detail: Between 5% and 10% below the high counts as a pullback, and the S&P 500 closed at 7,323.63 on Wednesday, about 6.3% below its record close of 7,818.93 on 6 October. It has now fallen five days running, its longest losing run since June; dips of this size happen in most years.
source: AP closing figures, 18 Nov; record close from Anadolu and EdgeX, 6 Oct

detail: Breadth was narrow on Tuesday: at midday CNBC counted 679 Nasdaq shares at new 52-week lows against 38 at new highs, with fallers outnumbering risers by about 2.7 to 1. When most shares fall together, the selling is wide rather than limited to a few big names.

Above 4.5% counts as high, and the US 10-year yield eased to about 5.06% on Wednesday from 5.10% as falling oil prices calmed inflation worries. Safe bonds paying over 5% set a high bar for shares to beat.

Markets expect rates to go up: futures fully price a quarter-point Fed rise on 9 December, and traders see about an 80% chance of a Bank of England rise on 17 December, down from 90% after UK inflation came in slightly below the Bank's forecast. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and tend to weigh on share prices, especially fast-growing companies.
source: Fed funds futures via Barchart, 18 Nov; LSEG data via Reuters, 18 Nov

detail: Above $90 a barrel counts as expensive, even after Brent crude settled 1.3% lower at $91.95 on Wednesday when US oil stocks rose more than expected. Dear oil keeps pressure on inflation, which is one reason central banks are raising rates.
source: ICE settlement via Reuters and Xinhua, 18 Nov
